sources: National Snow and Ice Data Center (nsidc.org)

cover.artAlt: A huge thunderstorm cloud towering over golden plains at sunset with a distant lightning bolt
cover.blurb: The sky puts on the biggest show on Earth, and it is free every single day. Turn the page and watch.

pages.title: Flash First, Then the Rumble
pages.artAlt: A single bright bolt of lightning over an empty landscape at dusk

facts.text: A lightning bolt is a giant spark of electricity. It heats the air around it to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, about five times hotter than the surface of the sun, and that air puffs outward so fast that the boom it makes is the thunder you hear.

Light reaches your eyes almost instantly, but sound takes its time getting to your ears. Count the seconds between the flash and the rumble, then divide by five, and that is roughly how many miles away the lightning was. Five seconds means about one mile.
facts.artAlt: A child at a window counts on their fingers while a bolt of lightning flashes over the houses outside
facts.caption: Count the seconds from the flash to the rumble, then divide by five.

facts.text: Thunder can usually be heard about 10 miles away. If you can hear it at all, that is the sky telling you to get inside a building, and once you are in, stay back from the windows and doors and wait with a grown-up until it has been quiet for a good half hour.
facts.artAlt: A tall dark storm cloud far off across open fields, with a curtain of rain falling beneath it and sunlit grass in the foreground
facts.caption: A storm this far off can still be loud enough to hear.

infographic.title: How hot is a lightning bolt?

rows.label: The air inside a lightning bolt

infographic.caption: Every number here is in degrees Fahrenheit. The bolt and the sun come from the National Weather Service, which says lightning heats the air about five times hotter than the sun's surface. The kitchen oven is an everyday hot thing, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: Sunlight Bent by Raindrops
pages.artAlt: A full rainbow arching over green hills after rain

facts.text: A rainbow needs two things at the same time: sunshine and raindrops still hanging in the air. White sunlight goes into a droplet, bends inside it, and comes back out split into all of its colors.

You can only see a rainbow with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. That is why they turn up after a shower when the sun is low, pointing your own shadow straight at the middle of the bow.
facts.artAlt: A person stands with their back to the low evening sun, their long shadow stretching toward a rainbow in the rainy sky ahead of them
facts.caption: Sun behind you, rain in front of you, shadow pointing at the bow.

facts.text: The colors always come in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. People remember it as a name, ROY G BIV. Look above a bright rainbow and you may spot a fainter second one with its colors in the opposite order.
facts.artAlt: A double rainbow over wet fields, the bright lower bow with red on the outside and a fainter second bow above it with its colors flipped
facts.caption: The fainter upper bow wears its colors the other way around.

infographic.title: How a rainbow gets made

stops.label: The sun shines low behind you while rain is still falling in front of you
Sunlight goes into a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back, and bends again coming out
The bent light spreads into all its colors and paints a bow across the sky

infographic.caption: No numbers in this one, just the three things that have to happen, in order. The steps come from the UCAR Center for Science Education.

pages.title: The Calm Eye of the Storm
pages.artAlt: A hurricane seen from space as a huge white spiral with a clear round eye in the middle

facts.text: A hurricane is an enormous spinning pile of thunderstorms. From a satellite up in space it looks like a pinwheel, with curved rainbands of cloud spiraling in toward the middle.

The hole in the center is called the eye, and it is usually about 20 to 40 miles across. Inside it the air sinks, the wind drops to a light breeze, and the sky can be clear enough to see stars straight overhead while the storm turns all around it.
facts.artAlt: A close satellite view of a hurricane's round eye, a clear dark hole ringed by towering white walls of cloud
facts.caption: Inside the eye the wind drops and the sky can open right up.

facts.text: Ringing the eye is the eyewall, a circle of very tall thunderstorms where the rain and wind are strongest. Special planes with scientists on board fly right through it to measure the storm, so forecasters can tell everyone what is coming days ahead.
facts.artAlt: A four-engine hurricane hunter airplane flying in front of a huge dark wall of storm cloud
facts.caption: Hurricane hunter planes fly straight through the eyewall to measure the storm.

infographic.title: How wide is the eye of a hurricane?

rows.label: The calm eye in the middle
An hour of driving on the highway

infographic.caption: The eye and the whole storm are measured by NOAA. The hour of driving is an everyday distance, here only so you have something to measure against.

pages.title: Six Sides, Every Single Time
pages.artAlt: Close-up of tiny snowflakes resting on a dark blue mitten

facts.text: Every snowflake has six sides. As water freezes, its tiny building blocks lock together in a repeating six-sided pattern, and the whole crystal grows outward following that same rule.

The temperature decides the shape. Near 23 degrees Fahrenheit crystals grow long and needle-like, and near 5 degrees Fahrenheit they grow flat and plate-like, so one snowstorm can drop several different styles of flake.
facts.artAlt: Magnified snow crystals on dark cloth, thin needle-shaped ones lying beside flat six-sided plate-shaped ones
facts.caption: Colder air or warmer air grows a whole different shape of flake.

facts.text: No two flakes look quite the same because no two take the same trip down. Each one drifts through slightly different air on the way, and every wobble changes how it grows. The six arms on one flake match each other because they traveled together.
facts.artAlt: An extreme close-up of one snow crystal on a dark wool mitten, its six feathery arms matching each other exactly
facts.caption: Six arms, one trip down, all growing to match.

infographic.title: How tiny is one snow crystal?
